title: How seriously should we take Donald Kaufman's speech in the swamp in Adaptation (2002)?

commenti.body: [removed]

charlie kaufman's movies have always been deeply weird and experimental, but what makes him so great is the emotional core that runs in his movies. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind wouldn't be great if it was only Jim Carrey running around his subconscious, its great because of the emotional journey he and Kate Winslet go on. 

I don't think Adaptation is making fun of you, I think it agrees with you.

> And certainly I think that IS the intention, or at least partially.

It is as the whole movie is.  A screenwriter struggling with screenwriting and being a screenwriter, and writing about that is selfish, solipsistic, and "kinda weird."

I think it's definitely meant to be taken seriously because it's coming from the character Charlie felt superior to the entire film because of his status and intelligence concerning his craft and the one who finally helps him realize the epiphany he's been desperately searching for the entire film.  It doesn't matter if it's the cliche' of all cliche's.  Charlie couldn't see it, hear it, feel it.  He sees it, hears it, feels it when Donald says it and that allows him to move forward.  

We're forever looking for the thing that will move us.  I do it every day.  We all have the idioms, proverbs, sayings that help us in life and can live that way and most of the time we choose not to despite knowing better.  I think because, as you were talking about, it doesn't necessarily click.  We're looking for the click, the strike from the match that starts the fire.

"And I think Adaptation also tries to deal with that notion of shifting and throwing people off balance. People are very critical of Adaptation’s ending, they think of the end as a failure. But one thing I’ve never seen in print is that that movie was intended to be a failure. Then, rather than make it about failure, which is a safe way to do it, I wanted the film to be a failure. That’s what happens; it’s about panicking and compromising, among other things. But when you’re watching the story play out, the writing of the screenplay, which is what you’re watching, it ends with an enormous compromise, and it’s a disaster, literally and figuratively. The character in that movie is the script, that’s the character you’re following, not the people. And I guess people can’t feel an emotional connection to a screenplay. But I thought it reflected a corruption of the man who was writing it."

https://reverseshot.org/interviews/entry/332/charlie-kaufman

there are other interviews with him about this if you'd like to read more about the process of writing adaptation or his thoughts about it...

I always thought the alligator was the deus ex machina. 

I never made the connection to Donald's speech being the "easy moral resolution," but even if that's what it's intended to be I don't think that detracts from the wisdom that's conveyed by his words. I watched that movie back when it first came out, when I was young and overly-concerned with the impression that I thought I was making on people, and I also took something away from that scene about being less self-conscious. 

I think Charlie Kaufman's movies, as someone else already mentioned, have a strong emotional intelligence.

>I always thought the alligator was the deus ex machina.

Oh wow, that makes way more sense. Thank you!

The only thing really contributing to his self-worth was his status as a screenwriter. He knew what narrative things people responded to. The way other people react to the world emotionally had become an intellectual exercise for him. Valuing his own emotions and acting on those values wasn't within his perspective, at all.

To me, the 'gee-shucks' element of the ending is gratifying because it shows Charlie isn't committing his entire self-esteem on the implicit brilliance of his unconventional script. Is it structurally perfect? No, it's intentionally emotion-over-plot, in a movie that started very much plot-over-emotion, so there's no real 'bookend' feeling to be had. But Charlie seems to realize that he hasn't actually *lived* a lot of the things he's trying to write, and it's a victory over his maladaptive intellectualizing defense mechanism to simply prefer genuine, simple emotion attached to a simple story.

I recall David Foster Wallace talking about addiction recovery and how all of the sayings, e.g. "one day at a time" come off as totally trite and meaningless, until you're working through the program and at some point something shifts and you feel one of those sayings that you've heard a million times on a bone deep level. The framing is often what makes the difference. If you felt it, it's capital T True, and it wouldn't matter even if the film was making fun of you (though I don't think it was). How the movie feels is its business, not yours, or vice versa.
I feel that the structure *is* perfect because it perfectly reflects the themes of the story.

The third act is obviously making fun of mawkish, convenient, clichéd conclusions to stories which are about something much more complicated, and how difficult it can be to squeeze that type of complexity into a generic Hollywood ending, and still retain what made it special in the first place. 

Which is why the ending had those vapid slogans which are there to make people feel good, rather than to make them think. Obviously Charlie Kaufman is also making fun of his own failure to fully complete the artistic project he began, thus he does this whole meta thing with his twin brother.

People still find emotional resonance in it, because a lot of people are looking for self-reinforcement in art, comfortable sayings which tucks them in at night and tells them they're valid, smart, loved and too self critical. The obvious problem with that type of writing is that it turns into generic fluff which has nothing to do with the real worlds. Which is why the two very real people Charlie is adapting turn into a Noir psycho killer couple in a huge conspiracy. It's a massive disrespect to them as people, but it's necessary if people want the safe, generic ending where the heroic sacrifice ends with some zaccharine platitudes.

I fully agree with your interpretation. Is Donald's dramatic third-act monologue the exact sort of ending that Charlie hates? Yes - but it's also like, the absolute best possible version of that ending/speech. It may be "Hollywood"y, but it's still a fantastic speech. Which is why it resonates with Charlie and, as you mentioned, perhaps convinces him that maybe the mainstream way of doing things isn't always so bad after all.

Charlie'a character changes/grows over the course of the film, and Donald's speech being genuinely moving is a big part of why.

It’s definitely not sincere. Kaufman pretty much gives the game away in this quote from an interview published before he made Adaptation:

 “I hate a movie that will end by telling you that the first thing you should do is learn to love yourself. That is so insulting and condescending, and so meaningless. My characters don't learn to love each other or themselves."

The fact that Adaptation ends with a character expressing this sentiment indicates that Charlie Kaufman the character has completely compromised all of his artistic integrity in writing the screenplay. That comes through more clearly in the script itself, but Spike Jonze wanted the ending to be a little less absurd and toned down certain elements which made the intent more obvious.

> The third act is obviously making fun of mawkish, convenient, clichéd conclusions to stories which are about something much more complicated,

Yes, and consider Charlie-the-character's earlier line: "I don't want to cram in sex or guns or car chases or characters learning profound life lessons or growing or coming to like each other or overcome obstacles to succeed in the end." When in fact the third act does every single one of those things.

The third act is not just making fun of those cliched conclusions, it's making fun of creators and audiences both *expect* those cliches despite knowing that life isn't that way.
Exactly, it's a funny joke ending, but it's a little odd to see how far over everyone's heads it's gone.

Throught the entire film Charlie is miserable, utterly consumed by fear of what other people think about him. I mean we literally start the film with him assuming the person he just met detests him for a litany of minute reasons. This fear also causes him to be an unpleasant person to be around, he makes everyone he meets feel uncomfortable, depressed or angry.

Donald on the other hand is always exuding pure joy, he's kind to everyone including his brother who is constantly belittling him. People in turn like him and enjoy spending time around Donald.

So it strikes me as the film is showing how one mentality is obviously more appealing than the other, even if it can come across as "cringy"

(By the way I think you would find very interesting David Foster Wallace's speech This is Water, which deals with this topic)

> Anyway, I think we can all agree that the movie's tonal change in the last act is based on Donald "taking over" the script. That doesn't seem up for debate.

It is up for debate.

> and the fact that Charlie realizes in that moment that the "overused tropes" (in filmmaking and in life) can actually be "good" and "deep".

No. No, they are not. Again this is related to the issue above of it being up for debate. 

> What do you think? Is the speech meant to be taken seriously? Or is it just meant to make fun of the "easy" Hollywood ending?

As intended, it is neither but strongly leaning towards the latter especially based on mass or (I guess cult views here on r/truefilm but I'm a lurker first, poster 2nd so I'm sure someone will debate me on this claim.)

I never thought of it this way but I think I agree completely. Honestly every time I watch that movie I appreciate the third act shift more and more. Probably time for another rewatch after reading this.

But this is just it, I think it is more than a **joke** ending. Saying is it a joke ending suggests that we can just dismiss it. It is something we laugh **at** and then discard**. "**Haha, Charlie Kaufman is making fun of Hollywood tropes and the people who like those tropes."

To me, the point of the ending is not just "isn't it funny that Charlie Kaufman became what he hated". The point of the ending is that Charlie Kaufman learned that what he initially hated *actually* had value, and power, and a place. That is the emotional piece.

Sure it is poking fun at those tropes, but it is doing SO MUCH more than that. It is using those tropes not as an attack on Hollywood Tropes, but on Hollywood Postmodern Elitism too. It is saying "your feeling intellectual superiority is just as empty as this schlock." And that is the gray zone that gives it depth.

>Donald on the other hand is always exuding pure joy, he's kind to everyone including his brother who is constantly belittling him. People in turn like him and enjoy spending time around Donald.  
>  
>So it strikes me as the film is showing how one mentality is obviously more appealing than the other, even if it can come across as "cringy"

This is what makes the moment of revelation for Charlie so impactful to me. It is the fact that the answer is so *simple.* The reason Donald is so charming and joyful and kind is not because of some deep introspection or work that he is done. It isn't because he is naturally charming or because he worked hard to conquer some deep demons. It is just because his fundamental perspective is just different. It doesn't matter what she thinks, because that is her business, not mine. What a beautifully put, simple thought that changes *everything.*

Agreed, and well-said. Charlie spends the movie looking down on Donald and the cliche, nonsensical things Donald is writing. He's convinced that there's something deeper, more meaningful, more true... he just can't quite identify what exactly that is. All he knows is that it's not car chases, guns, etc.

And I think that's the flowers in the time lapse last scene: to the extent life has a deeper meaning beyond car chases and guns, great, it's there. Every day. And you don't have to go to the everglades or find the rarest of flowers. And it doesn't really matter if the third act of some movie even tries to capture this deeper meaning.

He makes fun of himself, definitely, but it's absolutely not like he actually found something valueable in the ending, the other way around. The ending is absolutely ridiculous and hokey, completely going away from any actual humanity or profundity that was in the original inspiration.

I don't really know what else to say, the ending takes two real vulnerable humans meeting each other in a way Charlie found to be surprisingly poigniant, and turned them into psycho-sexual murderers in a carchase, and then slaps on some schmaltzy nonsense at the end complete with a pop song and silly symbolism.

I mean, "Hollywood postmodern elitism"? It's pretty blatant the film is talking about how difficult it can be to make something new and creative, and the risk being that you sometimes can't complete it, Charlie's adaptation doesn't actually have an ending because he couldn't think of one, and it's talking about the allure of slapping a completely non-fitting nonsense ending onto it, because that's the kind of ending you can just slap on to any kind of story and have it be satisfying to a mainstream audience, because they're not really thinking about what's going on, they'd rather have the character explain out loud what's going on.

I don't wanna insult you, but I don't think you recognized the ending including the silly dying monologue, is playing it completely for laughs. If Charlie actually benefitted from the advice, he'd have created someting fitting and worthwhile and valueable, instead he ended up with complete nonsense, but at least he finished it. That's the real dilemma of the film, not whether Hollywood nonsense is valueable or not, the film is clear that it's really not.
good call, RIP DFW

It's more powerful for being both.  

Within the confines of the movie, Donald sort of remains both a corny guy and someone who enjoys himself a lot more and tends to be more fun and easier to be around than Charlie, but sort of also sets things in motion with that speech that allow for a kind of Jungian shadow/persona synthesis to let some of the better parts of Donald live on in Charlie - at least as I remember interpreting it at the time.  It's been a long time since I've seen it.  

In real life you also get to carry both.  Working as a therapist I think it's often more effective talking to people who struggle with issues like you're talking about to take both sides of it, accepting the part you want to push away from, and so on.  Doing so can sound very different than "just be happy with yourself".  There's also a bit of "how she felt was *her* business, not mine" that sounds like it acknowledges more of the interpersonal aspect of it than trite sayings like "just be happy with yourself" that try to pretend like we can squash it out of existence.  "That was *her* business" acknowledges that she can have business that's real and exists in the world *and* you don't have to know about it or *make* it yours.

That even kind of extends to how anxiety is conceived of in general - most of the DSM diagnosis tends to read as "*I'm* an anxious person", not "these ways I feel stuck relating to other people make me anxious".  I wonder if part of what's poignant for you and for others like me about the speech is that Donald gets across the maturity to let someone else actually be another independent person in a way that Charlie's constant preoccupations sort of don't.

I dunno.  Just one take on it.
It’s doing fine, even some In N Out Burgers  in Fort Worth.

If anything, Charlie Kaufman is poking fun at people who overthink things and forget to enjoy the simple things about life and art, which are plenty “deep” and poignant enough on their own. He certainly sees himself in that camp of overthinkers, and Adaptation is sort of a reminder for all of us who have that tendency to slow down.

One of the lessons i took from Infinite Jest was, "Sometimes the truth is simple to understand, but difficult to accept."

I think everyone believes they are special and that "what works for most people won't work for me". But the harder truth to accept is that the truth is very simple and straightforward and you just don't want to believe you are failing in the same way many many other people have.
This is completely ignoring the scene where Robert McKee calls out Kaufman’s flawed understanding of life. The “You don’t know crap about life” monologue is a refutation of his entire philosophy.

Charlie Kaufman doesn’t actually like Robert McKee’s philosophy of screenwriting. That much is obvious from every interview he’s given. Kaufman has talked about the true heart of the movie lying in how the screenplay itself is ruined, and the fact that “Charlie” takes on board McKee’s lessons is one of the signs that he’s failed to create something meaningful.

Not his entire philosophy, but Kaufman absolutely agrees that his original goals with adapting The Orchid Thief were impossible. You can’t make a successful film where nothing happens. It’s not entertaining, and it also isn’t reflective of the real world. Kaufman is acknowledging his own lack of awareness and limited perspective in the film. 

Does the movie become the exact opposite of his original intentions? Of course however, that’s because his original intentions were flawed. To say that Donald’s ending speech is purely satirical and void of meaning just isn’t true.

Well obviously the movie is what it is and we can interpret it however we want, but I think Kaufman has made his intention clear. How would you square your perspective with the Reverse Shot interview snipped posted by kurisona above?
